column2: The word comes from the Latin "salarium". A popular story says Roman soldiers were paid in salt, though historians say the link is uncertain.
The word is a contraction of the 16th-century phrase "God be with ye". Over time it shortened, influenced by "good day".
In Middle English, "nice" meant silly or ignorant, from the Latin "nescius". Its meaning shifted many times before becoming "pleasant".
column3: Words can flip their meaning entirely.

column2: In 14th-century Venice, ships from plague areas had to wait 40 days before landing. The Italian "quaranta giorni" means forty days.
Unlike French, which has the Académie française, English has no official body deciding its rules. Dictionaries record usage rather than dictate it.
column3: English grows by use, not decree.

column1: Robot comes from a Czech play
column2: Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. introduced the word. It comes from "robota", meaning forced labour.

column1: The dot over an i is called a tittle
column2: The small mark over a lowercase i or j is a tittle. It is thought to be where the phrase "to a T" may come from, though that is debated.
It comes from the Latin "musculus", little mouse. Romans thought flexing muscles looked like mice moving under the skin.
column3: Body words are full of animal pictures.

column2: It comes from the Italian "disastro", from "dis" (bad) and "astro" (star). Disasters were once blamed on the stars.

column1: Clue comes from a ball of thread
column2: A "clew" was a ball of yarn. In Greek myth, Theseus used thread to find his way out of the labyrinth, so a clew became something that guides you.

column1: Shakespeare is credited with many new words
column2: Words like "lonely", "swagger" and "bedroom" first appear in print in his works. Some may simply have been recorded first by him.
column3: First written is not always first said.

column2: In 1839, Boston newspapers had a fad for comic abbreviations. "OK" stood for "oll korrect", a deliberate misspelling of "all correct".
The Hawaiian alphabet uses five vowels and eight consonants, including the ʻokina glottal stop. Words often repeat sounds.
column3: Small alphabets can carry rich languages.

column2: One theory says it comes from the French "sabot", a wooden clog, linked to workers clumping or disrupting work. The exact origin is debated.
column3: Etymology is often a best guess.

column1: Avocado comes from an Aztec word
column2: The Nahuatl word "āhuacatl" was adapted by Spanish speakers into "aguacate", which became "avocado" in English.

column1: The longest English word in major dictionaries is a lung disease
column2: Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis has 45 letters. It was coined in 1935, partly to be the longest word.
column3: Some words exist just to be records.

column1: Bless you is said in many languages
column2: Many cultures have a response to sneezing, such as "Gesundheit" in German, meaning health. The customs probably grew from wishing good health.

column1: Handicap came from a betting game
column2: Hand in cap was a 17th-century trading game. It later described evening out horse races, then disadvantages in general.
column3: Words travel far from their origins.

column1: Ketchup may come from a fish sauce
column2: One theory traces it to a Hokkien Chinese word for a fermented fish sauce. Tomatoes were added much later.

column1: Some languages have no words for left and right
column2: Guugu Yimithirr in Australia uses compass directions instead, such as north and south. Speakers keep a constant sense of orientation.
column3: Language can shape how we think about space.

column1: Alphabet comes from its first two letters
column2: It comes from Greek "alpha" and "beta", the first two letters of the Greek alphabet. The Greeks adapted them from Phoenician letters.

column1: Hazard came from a dice game
column2: Hazard was a medieval dice game, likely from an Arabic word for dice. The meaning shifted from chance to danger.

column1: The ampersand was once a letter
column2: & comes from a ligature of "et", Latin for "and". Children once recited it at the end of the alphabet as "and per se and".

column1: Deadline was once a real line
column2: In the American Civil War, a deadline was a boundary in some prison camps that prisoners could not cross. Later it moved into printing and journalism.
column3: Some everyday words have dark origins.

column1: Mandarin uses tones to change meaning
column2: In Mandarin, the syllable "ma" can mean mother, hemp, horse or scold, depending on its tone. There are four main tones plus a neutral one.
It comes from the Old English "hlafweard", meaning guardian of the loaf. "Lady" comes from "hlæfdige", loaf-kneader.
column3: Power once meant controlling the bread.

column1: Bankrupt comes from a broken bench
column2: It is linked to the Italian "banca rotta", meaning broken bench. Moneylenders worked at benches, and a broken one signalled failure.
column3: Business failure has a vivid history.

column2: Bethlem Royal Hospital in London, a psychiatric hospital, was nicknamed Bedlam. The word came to mean chaos.
column3: Place names can turn into everyday words.

column2: A popular story says it means "without wax", from sculptors hiding flaws. Most scholars trace it to Latin "sincerus", meaning pure.
It comes from the Greek "tragōidia", possibly from "tragos", goat, and "ōidē", song. Why goats is still debated.
It comes from the Old Norse "vindauga", combining wind and eye.

column1: Nightmare involves a goblin, not a horse
column2: The "mare" in nightmare comes from an Old English word for a spirit that sat on sleepers' chests.
column3: Similar sounds can hide different meanings.

column2: It comes from Old English "dægesēage", because the flower opens in the morning and closes at night.
The pupil of the eye comes from Latin "pupilla", little doll, after the tiny reflection you see of yourself in someone's eye.
From Latin "com", with, and "panis", bread. A companion is someone you share bread with.
It comes from the Greek "sarkazein", to tear flesh, later meaning to sneer.

column1: Hello became popular with the telephone
column2: Thomas Edison is credited with promoting "hello" as a telephone greeting. Alexander Graham Bell preferred "ahoy".

column1: Emoji is not related to emotion
column2: It comes from Japanese "e", picture, and "moji", character. The resemblance to "emotion" is a coincidence.

column1: Panic comes from the god Pan
column2: Pan was a Greek god of the wild, said to cause sudden fear in travellers.
column3: Gods live on in our vocabulary.

column2: It comes from Ceres, the Roman goddess of agriculture and grain.
The cloth is linked to Genoa in Italy, called "Gênes" in French. Denim comes from "de Nîmes", a French town.
It is named after Tuxedo Park, New York, where the jacket became fashionable in the 1880s.
A famous story says it was invented for a bet in Dublin. Historians find no evidence and the real origin is unclear.
column3: Some origin stories are too good to be true.

column2: In Old English, "sælig" meant happy or blessed. Over centuries it shifted to innocent, then foolish.
column3: Meanings can drift a long way.

column1: Awful once meant full of awe
column2: It originally meant inspiring wonder or fear. It now usually means very bad.
It comes from Old French "mort", dead, and "gage", pledge. The pledge dies when the debt is paid or the property is taken.

column1: Girl once meant any young person
column2: In Middle English, "gyrle" could refer to a young person of either sex.

column1: Pedigree comes from a crane's foot
column2: It comes from French "pied de grue", crane's foot, because family tree lines looked like a bird's foot.
It comes from "al-jabr", from the title of a 9th-century book by the mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
column3: Maths carries history in its words.

column1: Algorithm comes from a person's name
column2: It derives from al-Khwarizmi, whose name was Latinised as Algoritmi.

column1: Checkmate means the king is helpless
column2: It comes from Persian "shāh māt", often translated as "the king is helpless" or "the king is stuck".
It comes from the Greek "hippos", horse, and "potamos", river.
In English, "pineapple" first meant a pine cone. The tropical fruit took the name because of its resemblance.
It came via Dutch "koffie" from Turkish "kahve", from Arabic "qahwa".
column3: A word can journey as far as the bean.

column2: Catsup and catchup were common spellings. Ketchup became standard over the 20th century.
column3: Spelling can be settled by markets.

column1: Serendipity comes from a fairy tale
column2: Horace Walpole coined it in 1754, after the Persian tale The Three Princes of Serendip.
column3: Lucky discoveries got a lucky name.

column1: Nerd may come from Dr Seuss
column2: The word appears in Dr Seuss's 1950 book If I Ran the Zoo. Its later slang use spread from the US.
It comes from the 1938 play Gas Light and its film versions, where a husband manipulates his wife.

column1: Spam email is named after a sketch
column2: Monty Python's 1970 sketch has a café where Spam is in everything. The repetition inspired the name for junk messages.

column1: Bluetooth is named after a king
column2: It is named after Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century Danish king who united tribes, as the technology unites devices.
A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros. The company's name is a playful misspelling.
column3: A typo can become a giant brand.

column1: Lol is in the Oxford English Dictionary
column2: LOL was added to the OED in 2011. Internet language now shapes mainstream English.
Around 80 percent of English vocabulary is estimated to be borrowed. Latin and French gave large shares.

column1: Schadenfreude has no single English word
column2: German combines "Schaden", harm, and "Freude", joy, to mean pleasure at others' misfortune.
column3: Some languages name feelings others cannot.

column2: The Danish word for cosiness and contentment became popular in English around 2016.
column3: Words can export a way of life.

column1: The most common letter in English is E
column2: E appears in English text more than any other letter, around 12 percent of the time.

column1: Q is almost always followed by "U"
column2: In English words, Q is nearly always followed by U. Exceptions often come from other languages, like "qi".

column1: Some words are their own opposites
column2: Sanction can mean allow or penalise. "Dust" can mean remove dust or add it. These are called contronyms.

column1: Bookkeeper has three double letters in a row
column2: It has oo, kk and ee consecutively. "Bookkeeping" does too.
The nine-letter word has just one vowel. It is one of the longest English words like that.

column1: Set has a huge number of meanings
column2: The Oxford English Dictionary lists hundreds of senses for "set", though "run" has overtaken it in some counts.
The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog contains every letter of the alphabet. It was used to test typewriters.

column1: The dot-com era gave us new words
column2: Words like "email", "website" and "download" became everyday English in the 1990s.
Japanese uses kanji, hiragana and katakana, often together in a single sentence.
Finnish nouns change form in many ways to express meaning that English shows with prepositions.

column1: Some languages have no word for blue
column2: Several languages historically used one word for both blue and green. Linguists call this "grue".
British Sign Language and American Sign Language are distinct, each with its own grammar.

column1: The word "the" is the most common in English
column2: The is the most frequently used word in written English.
column3: The smallest words do the most work.

column1: Okay is one of the most widely understood words
column2: OK is used and understood in many languages around the world.
Apples and pears means stairs, and often only the first word is used: "up the apples".
column3: Slang can be a secret code.

column2: Both trace back to the Nahuatl "āhuacatl". Guacamole adds "mōlli", meaning sauce.
From Latin "trivium", where three roads meet. Gossip at crossroads came to mean small, everyday matters.
column3: Small talk has a street address.

column2: The Italian greeting comes from the Venetian "s'ciavo", meaning I am your servant.
column3: Politeness can wear down into a casual hello.

column2: From Old French "cuevrefeu", a medieval signal to cover hearth fires for the night.
column3: Safety rules leave traces in language.
